38.t: Gog and Magog: a vision of a final assault by the nations on God's restored people, ending in God's decisive victory. Revelation 20:8 takes up the names for the last battle.

39.t: Gog and Magog: a vision of a final assault by the nations on God's restored people, ending in God's decisive victory. Revelation 20:8 takes up the names for the last battle.

1:1.t: "The thirtieth year": probably Ezekiel's age, the age at which priests began their service (Numbers 4:3). The fifth year of Jehoiachin's exile (verse 2) was 593 BC. The Kebar River (the KJV's "Chebar") was a canal near Nippur in Babylonia.

1:4.t: "Glowing metal": the KJV's "amber"; the Hebrew chashmal is uncertain, perhaps an alloy of gold and silver.

1:22.t: "Vault": the KJV's "firmament", the same word as in Genesis 1:6.

3:15.t: Tel Aviv (the KJV's "Tel-abib") means "mound of the flood" or "hill of grain". It was a settlement of exiles in Babylonia; the modern city took its name from this verse.

4:1.t: "A block of clay": the KJV's "a tile", a soft clay brick used for writing.

4:5.t: The 390 days and 40 days are years of Israel's and Judah's sin. The Greek reads 190 days.

4:11.t: "About half a liter": the KJV's "the sixth part of an hin", about 0.6 liters.

6:14.t: "From the desert to Diblah": the KJV's "more desolate than the wilderness toward Diblath". Diblah may be Riblah in the north; the phrase means from one end of the land to the other.

7:7.t: "Doom": the KJV's "The morning"; the Hebrew tsephirah is uncertain.

7:17.t: "Every leg will be wet with urine": the KJV's "all knees shall be weak as water".

7:22.t: "The place I treasure": the KJV's "my secret place", the temple.

8:1.t: The sixth year of Jehoiachin's exile was 592 BC.

8:3.t: "The idol that provokes to jealousy": the KJV's "the image of jealousy", an idol in the temple court that stirred God's jealous anger (Deuteronomy 32:16).

8:14.t: Tammuz: a Mesopotamian god of vegetation, whose death was mourned each summer.

8:17.t: "Putting the branch to their nose": a pagan rite whose meaning is uncertain.

9:2.t: "A writing kit": the KJV's "a writer's inkhorn".

10:3.t: "South side": the KJV's "right side"; facing east, the right is south.

10:13.t: "The whirling wheels": the KJV's "O wheel"; Hebrew galgal.

10:14.t: "The face of a cherub": in 1:10 it is called the face of an ox.

11:3.t: "The time is not near to build houses": the KJV's "It is not near; let us build houses". The Hebrew can be read either way. The leaders boasted that they were the choice meat, safe inside the pot of Jerusalem.

11:16.t: "For a little while I have been a sanctuary for them": the KJV's "yet will I be to them as a little sanctuary". Without the temple, God Himself was present with the exiles.

11:23.t: "The mountain east of it": the Mount of Olives.

12:13.t: Fulfilled when King Zedekiah was captured, blinded and taken to Babylon (2 Kings 25:4-7).

13:10.t: "Whitewash": the KJV's "untempered morter", a coat that makes a weak wall look sound.
"Peace, when there is no peace": see Jeremiah 6:14.

13:18.t: "Magic charms ... veils": the KJV's "pillows ... kerchiefs". The exact objects are uncertain; they were used in magic to control people's lives.

14:14.t: "Daniel": the Hebrew spelling is Dan'el, which may refer to Daniel the exile (Daniel 1-6) or to an ancient righteous man known from Canaanite literature. Noah, Daniel and Job were famous for righteousness that saved others or survived disaster.

15:2.t: The wood of a vine is too weak for building and fit only for fuel; Israel, God's vine (Isaiah 5, Psalm 80), has become useless.

16:3.t: "Your ancestry and birth": Jerusalem was a Canaanite city (the Jebusites) before David took it.

16:10.t: "Fine leather": the KJV's "badgers' skin"; see Exodus 25:5.

16:26.t: "With large genitals": the KJV's "great of flesh". The language is deliberately shocking, mocking Judah's alliances with Egypt.

16:29.t: "Babylonia, a land of merchants": the KJV's "the land of Canaan unto Chaldea"; the Hebrew kena'an can also mean "merchants".

16:46.t: "To the north ... to the south": the KJV's "at thy left hand ... at thy right hand"; facing east, left is north and right is south.

16:57.t: "Syria": the KJV's reading; some Hebrew manuscripts and the Syriac read "Edom".

17:3.t: The first eagle is Nebuchadnezzar; the top of the cedar is King Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC (verse 12).

17:5.t: The seedling is Zedekiah, made king by Nebuchadnezzar (verse 13).

17:7.t: The second eagle is Pharaoh of Egypt, to whom Zedekiah turned (verse 15).

17:16.t: Zedekiah's broken oath had been sworn in the LORD's name (2 Chronicles 36:13).

18:6.t: "Eat at the mountain shrines": the KJV's "eaten upon the mountains", sharing in idolatrous sacrificial meals.

18:8.t: "Lend at interest": the KJV's "given forth upon usury". See Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:36.

19:1.t: "Princes": the last kings of Judah. The first lion cub is Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt (2 Kings 23:31-34); the second is probably Jehoiachin or Zedekiah, taken to Babylon.

19:10.t: "In your vineyard": the KJV's "in thy blood"; the Hebrew is uncertain.

20:1.t: The seventh year of exile was 591 BC.

20:29.t: "Bamah": the Hebrew word for "high place", with a mocking wordplay: "What (mah) is the high place to which you go (ba'im)?"

20:39.t: "But afterward you will surely listen to Me": the KJV reads "and hereafter also, if ye will not hearken unto me". The Hebrew is uncertain.

20:46.t: "The south ... the southland": the KJV's "the south ... the south field". Three different Hebrew words are used; the third, negev, is the southern region of Judah.

21:10.t: The Hebrew of these verses is very difficult, and translations differ widely.

21:13.t: The Hebrew of these verses is very difficult, and translations differ widely.

21:21.t: "Cast lots with arrows": the KJV's "he made his arrows bright"; marked arrows were drawn from a quiver to decide a course. "Examine the liver": reading signs in the liver of a sacrificed animal was a common Babylonian practice.

21:25.t: The "profane and wicked prince" is King Zedekiah.

22:16.t: "When you have been defiled in the eyes of the nations": the KJV's "thou shalt take thine inheritance in thyself". The Hebrew can be read either way.

22:25.t: "Her princes": the KJV's "her prophets"; the Greek reads "princes", as in verse 27.

23:4.t: Oholah means "her tent"; Oholibah means "My tent is in her". The names may hint at Jerusalem's temple and Samaria's rival shrines.

23:20.t: The language is deliberately coarse, to shock Judah into seeing how degrading its foreign alliances were.

23:23.t: Pekod, Shoa and Koa were peoples of the Babylonian empire.

23:42.t: "Drunkards": the KJV's "Sabeans"; the Hebrew can be read either way.

24:1.t: The tenth day of the tenth month of the ninth year was January 15, 588 BC, the day the final siege began (2 Kings 25:1). Jews still keep it as a fast day.

24:17.t: "Do not cover your mustache and beard": the KJV's "cover not thy lips", a sign of mourning (Leviticus 13:45, Micah 3:7).

25:16.t: Kerethites: the KJV's "Cherethims", a people related to the Philistines, perhaps from Crete.

26:1.t: "In the eleventh year, on the first day of the month": following the KJV and the Hebrew, which do not name the month. The eleventh year (587-586 BC) is the year Jerusalem fell.

26:7.t: Nebuchadnezzar besieged Tyre for thirteen years (about 586-573 BC). Alexander the Great later destroyed the island city in 332 BC, building a causeway with rubble from the mainland city, as verses 12 and 14 describe.

27:11.t: "With your army": the KJV's reading; the Hebrew cheleq may also be a place name, Helek.

27:15.t: "Dedan": following the KJV and the Hebrew; the Greek reads "Rhodians", the people of Rhodes.

27:17.t: "Confections": the KJV's "Pannag"; the meaning is uncertain.

27:18.t: "White wool. Dan and Greece, coming and going": following the KJV. The Hebrew is difficult; some read "wool from Zahar and casks of wine from Uzal".

28:13.t: Several of these stones cannot be identified with certainty. Nine of them appear among the twelve stones of the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17-20). "Garnet": the KJV's "carbuncle". "The settings and mountings of your jewels": the KJV's "the workmanship of thy tabrets and of thy pipes"; the Hebrew is uncertain.

29:3.t: "Monster": the KJV's "dragon"; Hebrew tannim, probably the crocodile of the Nile.

29:10.t: "From Migdol to Aswan": the KJV's "from the tower of Syene"; the Hebrew migdol means "tower". Migdol was in the north of Egypt and Syene (Aswan) in the south, so the phrase means "the whole of Egypt".

29:17.t: The twenty-seventh year (571 BC) is the latest date in Ezekiel.

30:5.t: "All Arabia": the KJV's "all the mingled people"; the Hebrew can be read either way. Kub is unknown.

30:13.t: "Memphis ... Thebes ... Pelusium ... Heliopolis ... Bubastis ... Tahpanhes": the KJV's "Noph ... No ... Sin ... Aven ... Pi-beseth ... Tehaphnehes".

31:3.t: "Consider Assyria": the KJV's "Behold, the Assyrian". Assyria, once a mighty cedar, had fallen to Babylon in 612-609 BC. Egypt will fall the same way.

31:15.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "the grave ... hell"; Hebrew Sheol.

32:2.t: "Monster": the KJV's "whale"; Hebrew tannim, probably the crocodile.

32:21.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "hell"; Hebrew Sheol.

32:27.t: "The realm of the dead": the KJV's "hell"; Hebrew Sheol.
"Their shields resting on their bones": the KJV reads "but their iniquities shall be upon their bones". The Hebrew avonotam (iniquities) may be a copying error for tsinnotam (shields).

33:21.t: The twelfth year, tenth month, fifth day is January 585 BC, about six months after Jerusalem fell. Some manuscripts read "eleventh year".

33:31.t: "Their mouths speak of love": the KJV's "with their mouth they shew much love". The Hebrew agavim means "passionate words".

34:3.t: "The curds": the KJV's "the fat"; the Hebrew can be read either way.

34:29.t: "A land renowned for its crops": the KJV's "a plant of renown".

35:2.t: Mount Seir: the mountains of Edom. Edom's long hostility to Israel went back to Esau and Jacob (Genesis 27:41).

37:16.t: Judah stands for the southern kingdom, Joseph and Ephraim for the northern kingdom of Israel.

38:2.t: "The chief prince of Meshech and Tubal": the KJV's reading. The Hebrew nesi rosh can also be read "prince of Rosh", as a place name. Gog is an unknown ruler; Magog, Meshech and Tubal were peoples of Asia Minor (Genesis 10:2).

39:2.t: "Leave only a sixth of you": the KJV's reading; the Hebrew shishe'tikha is uncertain and may mean "drag you along".

39:11.t: "The Sea": the Dead Sea. Hamon Gog means "the horde of Gog"; Hamonah (verse 16) means "horde".

39:26.t: "They will forget their shame": the KJV's "After that they have borne their shame"; the Hebrew can be read either way.

40:1.t: The twenty-fifth year of exile was 573 BC, fourteen years after Jerusalem fell. Chapters 40-48 are a vision of a new temple, a renewed priesthood and a restored land, to which the glory of God returns (43:1-5).

40:5.t: Measurements in chapters 40-48: the KJV gives them in cubits. Ezekiel's "long cubit" (a cubit and a handbreadth) is about 53 centimeters, and his measuring rod of six long cubits is about 3.2 meters. In this translation: 1 cubit is about half a meter; 1.5 cubits about 80 centimeters; 2 cubits about 1.1 meters; 3 about 1.6; 4 about 2.1; 5 about 2.7; 6 about 3.2; 7 about 3.7; 8 about 4.2; 10 about 5.3; 11 about 5.8; 13 about 6.9; 14 about 7.4; 20 about 10.5; 25 about 13; 50 about 27; 60 about 32; 70 about 37; 90 about 48; 100 about 53; 500 about 265 meters.

40:14.t: The Hebrew of this verse is difficult; the KJV reads "He made also posts of threescore cubits".

40:48.t: "The width of the gateway was about 1.6 meters on either side": following the KJV and the Hebrew. The Greek adds that the entrance itself was fourteen cubits (about 7.4 meters) wide.

41:22.t: "About 1.6 meters high and about 1.1 meters square": the KJV's "three cubits high, and the length thereof two cubits".

42:16.t: "Five hundred rods, about 1,600 meters": following the KJV and the Hebrew, "five hundred reeds". The Greek reads "five hundred cubits", about 265 meters, which fits the size of the temple area in 45:2.

43:7.t: "The funeral offerings for their kings": the KJV's "the carcases of their kings". The Hebrew pigre can mean corpses or memorial monuments.

43:13.t: The KJV's "settle" is a ledge of the altar. The KJV figures: two cubits, one cubit, four cubits (verses 14-15); twelve cubits square (verse 16); fourteen cubits square, with a border of half a cubit (verse 17).

44:2.t: The east gate stays shut because the glory of the LORD came in through it (43:4).

44:3.t: "The prince": the ruler of the restored community.

45:1.t: The Hebrew does not name the unit for these measurements. The KJV supplies "reeds" in verse 1; most interpreters understand cubits, which would make the sacred district about 13 kilometers by 5.3 kilometers. The section in verse 2 would then be about 265 meters square, matching 42:20 in the Greek.

45:10.t: "Ephah ... bath ... homer": dry and liquid measures. The ephah and the bath each held about 22 liters; the homer about 220 liters.

45:12.t: "Mina": the KJV's "maneh". The Hebrew text gives twenty, twenty-five and fifteen shekels, totaling sixty; the Greek reads fifty.

45:13.t: "About 3.7 liters from every 220 liters": the KJV's "the sixth part of an ephah of an homer".

45:14.t: "About 2.2 liters": the KJV's "the tenth part of a bath".

45:24.t: "About 22 liters ... about 3.7 liters of olive oil": the KJV's "an ephah ... an hin of oil".

46:5.t: "About 22 liters ... about 3.7 liters of oil": the KJV's "an ephah ... an hin of oil".

46:7.t: "About 22 liters ... about 3.7 liters of oil": the KJV's "an ephah ... an hin of oil".

46:11.t: "About 22 liters ... about 3.7 liters of oil": the KJV's "an ephah ... an hin of oil".

46:14.t: "About 3.7 liters of flour with about 1.2 liters of oil": the KJV's "the sixth part of an ephah, and the third part of an hin of oil".

46:17.t: "The year of freedom": the KJV's "the year of liberty", the Jubilee (Leviticus 25:10).

46:22.t: "About 21 meters long and 16 meters wide": the KJV's "forty cubits long and thirty broad".

47:8.t: "The Arabah ... the Dead Sea": the KJV's "the desert ... the sea".

47:10.t: "The Mediterranean Sea": the KJV's "the great sea". En Gedi and En Eglaim were springs by the Dead Sea.

47:15.t: "The Mediterranean Sea": the KJV's "the great sea". En Gedi and En Eglaim were springs by the Dead Sea.
"Lebo Hamath": the KJV's "as men go to Zedad; Hamath". Lebo Hamath means "the entrance to Hamath".

47:19.t: "The Mediterranean Sea": the KJV's "the great sea". En Gedi and En Eglaim were springs by the Dead Sea.
"Meribah Kadesh": the KJV's "the waters of strife in Kadesh".

48:1.t: As in 45:1-6, the Hebrew gives no unit for these measurements. The KJV supplies "reeds" in verse 8 and "measures" in verses 30-35. If cubits are meant, 25,000 is about 13 kilometers, 4,500 is about 2.4 kilometers and 18,000 is about 9.5 kilometers.

1:28.t: "The appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD": Ezekiel piles up careful words, "appearance", "likeness", to show that he saw a reflection, not God Himself. The glory (Hebrew kavod, "weight, splendor") is the visible presence of God, which Ezekiel will see leaving the temple (chapters 10-11) and returning (chapter 43).

2:1.t: "Son of man" (Hebrew ben-adam): "human being", used over ninety times for Ezekiel, stressing his weakness before God. Jesus took "the Son of Man" as His favorite title for Himself, drawing on Daniel 7:13.

2:2.t: "The Spirit came into me" (Hebrew ruach): the Spirit of God gives the prophet strength to stand and hear.

3:17.t: "A watchman" (Hebrew tsopheh): a lookout on the city wall who warns of danger. See 33:1-9.

6:7.t: "You will know that I am the LORD" (Hebrew vida'tem ki ani YHWH): Ezekiel's key refrain, used more than sixty times. Through judgment and through restoration, Israel and the nations will come to know who God truly is.

6:9.t: "I have been grieved by their adulterous hearts": the KJV's "I am broken with their whorish heart". Israel's idolatry is pictured as unfaithfulness in marriage, which wounds God's heart. See chapters 16 and 23.

9:4.t: "A mark" (Hebrew tav): the last letter of the Hebrew alphabet, which in the old script was written as an X or a cross. Those who grieved over sin were marked for protection, like the blood on the doorposts at Passover (Exodus 12:13). Compare Revelation 7:3 and 9:4.

9:6.t: "Begin at My sanctuary": judgment starts with those closest to God. See 1 Peter 4:17.

10:4.t: The departure of God's glory: step by step the glory of the LORD leaves the temple, first to the threshold, then to the east gate (10:19), then to the Mount of Olives (11:23). In 43:1-5 Ezekiel sees it return.

10:18.t: The departure of God's glory: step by step the glory of the LORD leaves the temple, first to the threshold, then to the east gate (10:19), then to the Mount of Olives (11:23). In 43:1-5 Ezekiel sees it return.

11:19.t: "An undivided heart ... a heart of flesh" (Hebrew lev echad ... lev basar): the KJV's "one heart". God promises to replace a hard, unresponsive heart with one that is alive to Him. See 36:26-27 and Jeremiah 31:33.

16:6.t: "Live!" (Hebrew chayi): God's word of life spoken over an abandoned newborn: Israel's existence was His gracious gift from the start.

16:8.t: "I spread the corner of My garment over you": a pledge of marriage and protection (Ruth 3:9). "You became Mine": the covenant at Sinai is pictured as a marriage.

16:49.t: "This was the sin of your sister Sodom": arrogance, excess and neglect of the poor, alongside the "detestable things" of verse 50 (Genesis 19).

16:60.t: "An everlasting covenant ... when I make atonement for you" (Hebrew bekhapperi): after the darkest picture of Jerusalem's unfaithfulness, God promises a covenant based on His own forgiveness. Grace, not judgment, has the last word. Compare Jeremiah 31:31-34.

17:22.t: "A tender sprig ... a splendid cedar": God Himself will plant a new shoot from David's line on Zion's mountain. Compare the "Branch" of Isaiah 11:1 and Jeremiah 23:5, and Jesus' parable of the mustard seed, where birds nest in its branches (Matthew 13:31-32).

18:4.t: "Everyone belongs to Me ... The one who sins is the one who will die" (Hebrew hannephesh hachote'th hi tamut): literally "the soul that sins, it shall die", as the KJV has it. Nephesh here means the living person. Each generation stands before God on its own; no one is doomed by a parent's sin or saved by a parent's goodness.

18:23.t: "Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?": God's deepest desire is for sinners to turn and live. See 33:11, 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9.

18:32.t: "Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?": God's deepest desire is for sinners to turn and live. See 33:11, 1 Timothy 2:4 and 2 Peter 3:9.

18:31.t: "Get a new heart and a new spirit": here God calls the people to change; in 36:26 He promises to do it for them.

20:9.t: "For the sake of My name": again and again God spared Israel, not because they deserved it, but to show His true character to the nations.

20:14.t: "For the sake of My name": again and again God spared Israel, not because they deserved it, but to show His true character to the nations.

20:22.t: "For the sake of My name": again and again God spared Israel, not because they deserved it, but to show His true character to the nations.

20:44.t: "For the sake of My name": again and again God spared Israel, not because they deserved it, but to show His true character to the nations.

20:11.t: "By which the person who obeys them will live": see Leviticus 18:5. Paul quotes this in Romans 10:5 and Galatians 3:12.

20:25.t: "Statutes that were not good": God gave the people over to the consequences of their own choices, even to the horrible practice of child sacrifice they had learned from the nations. Compare Romans 1:24-28.

20:37.t: "Pass under My rod": a shepherd counted his sheep as they passed under his staff, separating his own from the others (Leviticus 27:32).

21:27.t: "Until He comes to whom it rightfully belongs" (Hebrew ad bo asher lo hammishpat): the crown of David's line will be left vacant until the true King comes. This echoes Genesis 49:10, "until Shiloh comes", and points to the Messiah. Following this reading, the pronouns are capitalized.

22:30.t: "Stand before Me in the gap": an intercessor who, like Moses, stands in the breach of the broken wall (Psalm 106:23). God looked for one and found none; the New Testament presents Christ as the One who stands in the gap for His people (Hebrews 7:25).

23:31.t: "Your sister's cup": the cup of God's wrath; see Jeremiah 25:15.

24:16.t: "The delight of your eyes" (Hebrew machmad enekha): Ezekiel's wife. He was forbidden to mourn openly so that his silence would be a sign of the people's numb grief when the temple, "the delight of your eyes" (verse 21), was destroyed.

28:12.t: The lament over the king of Tyre uses images of Eden and of a guardian cherub to describe a ruler who was given glory and fell through pride. Many Christian interpreters, as with Isaiah 14:12-15, have seen here a picture of the fall of Satan, whose pride the king's mirrors.

28:14.t: "A guardian cherub" (Hebrew keruv hassokhekh): the KJV's "the anointed cherub that covereth". Cherubim guarded Eden (Genesis 3:24) and spread their wings over the ark (Exodus 25:20).

31:6.t: "All the birds of the sky nested in its boughs": compare Daniel 4:12 and Jesus' parable of the mustard seed (Matthew 13:32). Great empires offered shelter, but God alone decides who stands and who falls.

32:18.t: A tour of the underworld: the great nations that once spread terror now lie together in shame. Sheol levels all human pride. The New Testament reveals more fully what lies beyond death (Luke 16:19-31, 1 Corinthians 15).

33:11.t: "As surely as I live ... I take no pleasure in the death of the wicked": see 18:23 and 18:32.

34:2.t: "Shepherds": the kings and leaders of Israel. In the ancient Near East, kings were often called shepherds of their people.

34:11.t: "I Myself will search for My sheep": God will do what the faithless shepherds failed to do. Jesus applies this to Himself: "The Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost" (Luke 19:10), and "I am the good shepherd" (John 10:11-16).

34:23.t: "One Shepherd, My servant David": a future king from David's line, written long after David's death, pointing to the Messiah (37:24-25, Jeremiah 23:5, Hosea 3:5). Following this reading, His pronouns are capitalized.

34:25.t: "A covenant of peace" (Hebrew berit shalom): see 37:26 and Isaiah 54:10.

36:22.t: "Not for your sake ... but for the sake of My holy name": God's grace does not depend on Israel's deserving it; He acts to show the world who He truly is.

36:25.t: "I will sprinkle clean water on you ... a new heart ... My Spirit in you" (Hebrew ruchi etten beqirbekhem): cleansing, a new heart, and God's own Spirit living within, the inner renewal of the new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Jesus spoke of being "born of water and the Spirit" (John 3:5), and the New Testament describes the Spirit's coming to live in believers (Romans 8:9-11, Titus 3:5).

36:26.t: "A heart of flesh": a heart that is alive and responsive to God, instead of a "heart of stone", hard and dead. See 11:19.

37:1.t: The valley of dry bones: the Hebrew ruach means "breath", "wind" and "spirit", and all three meanings are at work here (verses 5, 9, 14). As God breathed life into Adam (Genesis 2:7), His Spirit will breathe new life into a nation that has given up hope. Jesus' words to Nicodemus about the wind and the Spirit echo this (John 3:8).

37:24.t: "My servant David will be King ... their Prince forever": see 34:23-24.

37:27.t: "My dwelling place will be with them" (Hebrew mishkani): see Revelation 21:3, "The dwelling place of God is with man."

40:46.t: "The sons of Zadok": the priestly line that stayed faithful when others went astray (44:15). Zadok served as priest under David and Solomon (1 Kings 1-2).

41:4.t: "The Most Holy Place" (Hebrew qodesh haqqodashim): literally "the holy of holies", the inner room where God's presence dwelt.

43:2.t: The return of the glory: the glory that left the temple through the east gate (10:18-19, 11:23) now returns the same way and fills the house. God promises to live among His people forever (verse 7). John's Gospel says of Jesus, "The Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen His glory" (John 1:14).

44:28.t: "I am to be the only inheritance the priests have": see Numbers 18:20 and Deuteronomy 18:1-2.

45:9.t: "Use accurate scales": justice in everyday trade is part of true worship. See Leviticus 19:35-36 and Amos 8:5.

47:1.t: The river from the temple: water flowing from God's house brings life wherever it goes, even turning the Dead Sea fresh. Joel 3:18 and Zechariah 14:8 share the picture; Jesus spoke of "rivers of living water" flowing from those who believe in Him (John 7:37-39); and Revelation 22:1-2 shows the river of life and the tree whose leaves are "for the healing of the nations".

47:22.t: Foreigners who live among Israel are to receive an inheritance as if native-born, a striking widening of God's people.

48:35.t: "The LORD Is There" (Hebrew YHWH shammah): the KJV margin gives "Jehovah-shammah". The book that began with the glory leaving the temple ends with a city named for God's abiding presence. Revelation 21:3 and 22:3-4 describe its fulfillment.
